newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices extend rally on tighter supply forecast.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices extend rally on tighter supply forecast.

text.p: Crude oil prices received a shot in the arm on Friday when the West's energy watchdog revised down its oil supply estimate for the rest of the year at a time when the prospect of Iraqi exports has receded further into the future.

The Paris-based International Energy Agency (IEA) revised its estimate of supply from producers outside the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) downwards by 300,000 barrels per day (bpd) for the second half of 1996.
By 1540 GMT, October futures for world benchmark Brent Blend were trading up 20 cents at 22.36 a barrel, just down from an intra-day high of $22.42 a barrel.
The oil market had moved up a dollar since Iraqi troops moved into Iraqi Kurdistan last week, prompting the United Nations to freeze an oil-for-food deal.

Under a May 20 agreement, sanctions-hit Iraq would be allowed limited oil sales worth $2 billion every six months to pay for food and medicines pending the lifting of the U.N. emabrgo imposed after Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990.

"There is clearly higher demand and lower than expected non-OPEC output combined with the loss of Iraqi oil...I would have thought the scene is set for further price strength," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of MC Securities Ltd.
Crude oil buyers had been relaxed in anticipation of the resumed Iraqi exports, which were due sometime in late September or early October, and had taken the risk of running short.
Improved refinery margins coupled with a rally in gas oil (heating oil) prices with the approaching Northern hemisphere winter caught many buyers on the hop and fed the crude rally.
With gas oil prices so strong, refiners can get more out of a barrel of crude as they switch from producing lighter products like gasoline in the summer to heating oil and diesel in the winter.

A sqeeze on IPE gas oil raised the prompt contract to a five-year high of Friday as traders prepared for the European Union's switch from October 1 to a more environmentally friendly grade with lower sulphur emissions.
Europe's gas oil pool, now 0.2 percent sulphur for both heating oil and diesel, will be split 60:40 into 0.2 percent for heating oil and 0.05 poercent for diesel from that date.
The IPE contract will continue to specify only 0.2 percent.
Some traders expecting a shortage of the 0.2 percent sulphur gas oil to cover futures deliveries went on a huge buying spree and helped to sustain the crude rally in the last week.

Oil prices are about $5 a barrel above levels this time last year and recent figures suggest crude oil from the North Sea, home of benchmark Brent Blend, will be lower than originally forecast because of delays in new fields coming on stream.
Dealers said the market was still vulnerable to news from Iraq and short-covering before the close on Friday could boost prices even further.
